newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Embattled Asian currencies weak and weary.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Asian currencies weak and weary.

text.p: Embattled Southeast Asian currencies were weak and weary on Tuesday after taking a battering at the hands of investors and speculators in frenzied trade the previous day.
Traders said there was little buying of the currencies on Tuesday morning, with many players easing off a little to mull over conflicting signals from central bankers and government officials.

Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday Kuala Lumpur would allow market forces to determine the value of the ringgit, a comment dealers said was expected to weight further on the currency.

But the ringgit regained some poise on talk Bank Negara had intervened in offshore markets overnight and possibly early on Tuesday, after the currency slid to a 33-month low of 2.5700 against the U.S. dollar.
Dealers said speculative funds sold the ringgit down to its lowest level since October 1994 after Anwar said on Monday the ringgit was still within a "reasonable range".
"There's speculation that Negara was in at the 2.5700 top through agents in Sydney time, as well as in London and New York," said a senior dealer at a European bank in Singapore.
He said U.S. funds were likely to now push the currency towards 2.6000 to the dollar, although the rise could slow as the market had already bought huge amounts of dollars.
But another European bank dealer said many in the market were still eager to sell ringgit for dollars and were likely to push the Malaysian currency down to 2.58 to the dollar.
"If it rebounds from there, it could go back below 2.53," he said.
The ringgit was at 2.5565/95 to the dollar at 0350 GMT against 2.5310/30 at its close in Kuala Lumpur on Monday.
Indonesian central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said he saw more scope for interest rate cuts if inflation fell, but that had a muted effect on the rupiah, dealers said.
"The market is moving more in response to the liquidity situation, which is a bit tight because some tax payments are due," a Singapore-based dealer said.
"At the moment, the rupiah is the only currency being spared by speculators. But once speculation in the ringgit has subsided, they will look towards the rupiah," he added.
He said there was a line-up of corporate orders for the dollar below 2,440, but rumours that state banks were looking to sell aggressively above 2,460 were limiting rupiah weakness.
Spot rupiah was at 2,446.0/49.0 at 0350 GMT against an opening 2,450/55.
The Thai baht had a subdued morning, largely due to a lack of interest after the Bank of Thailand (BOT) confirmed it had intervened to support the currency on Monday.
The BOT said the baht had fallen about 15 percent since it switched to a managed float on July 2 from the previous system of pegging the baht to a basket of currencies.
"The speculators got what they wanted with the de facto devaluation," a Singapore dealer said. But he said the dollar would be bought on any dips as Thailand's financial woes had not ended.
The baht was quoted at 29.920/29.970 to the dollar in domestic markets at 0350 GMT and at 29.850/950 offshore.
The Philippine peso recovered some ground but remained weak on the second trading day after its effective devaluation.
The peso was quoted at 29.000/30.000 at 0350 GMT against an opening at around 30 to the dollar.
